a: The Bronze Age collapse, which occurred around 1200-1150 BCE, was a sudden and mysterious event that brought down nearly every major civilization in the eastern Mediterranean. The exact causes remain debated by historians, but several factors likely combined to create a perfect storm of collapse. One major factor was the invasion of the 'Sea Peoples,' a group of raiders whose identity remains unknown but who attacked and destroyed cities across the region, including the Egyptian New Kingdom. Archaeological evidence shows widespread destruction of cities, with many sites burned or abandoned. Climate change may have played a role — tree ring and sediment core data suggest a period of drought and cooling that would have reduced agricultural yields and put pressure on populations. Earthquakes have also been proposed as a contributing factor, with some sites showing evidence of seismic destruction. The collapse of the international trade network was another critical factor — the Bronze Age economy depended on long-distance trade of tin and copper, and the disruption of these trade routes would have severely impacted the production of bronze, which was essential for tools, weapons, and armor. The political fragmentation of the region, with many small city-states and kingdoms competing for resources, may have made them more vulnerable to external attacks and internal conflicts. The collapse led to a 'dark age' in which writing systems disappeared, urban centers were abandoned, and literacy rates plummeted. The Greek Dark Ages that followed lasted for centuries until the emergence of new civilizations. The suddenness of the collapse, which occurred within a few decades, suggests that multiple factors may have interacted in a cascading series of failures that overwhelmed the resilience of Bronze Age societies.
